claims.text: Enhanced high-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed primarily by kinetic hindrance from reduced surface diffusion rather than solely by configurational entropy.
The proposed initial nanoalloys are disordered, compositionally uniform, multi-principal-element materials with nanoscale dimensions.
A surface-capping treatment can specifically slow surface atomic diffusion without changing overall composition or configurational entropy.
Systematically reducing nanoparticle size can slow surface atomic diffusion by increasing diffusion barriers.
The comparison will be conducted at 600–900 °C under an inert atmosphere and below melting or severe oxidation thresholds.
Surface diffusion mediates atomic rearrangements that drive phase coarsening or decomposition in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Surface treatment increases kinetic barriers to atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility limits diffusion-driven coarsening and phase changes.
Kinetic hindrance stabilizes the disordered phase even when the thermodynamic contribution from configurational entropy is unchanged.
Capped nanoalloys will exhibit slower grain growth than untreated nanoalloys under identical high-temperature conditions.
Smaller, purportedly diffusion-impaired particles will exhibit slower grain growth than standard-size untreated particles.
Diffusion-hindered nanoalloys will undergo less phase decomposition than untreated controls.
Diffusion-hindered nanoalloys will retain a more homogeneous chemical composition than untreated controls.
The prediction is restricted to similarly composed, initially disordered nanoalloys at temperatures that activate diffusion but remain below melting and severe oxidation.
The effect should be less distinguishable in bulk samples because surface and interface effects are diminished.
The relative contributions of kinetic and thermodynamic stabilization may vary in regimes where both mechanisms compete.
The magnitude of stability improvement may vary with the surface treatment and nanoparticle size distribution.
A lack of statistically significant reductions in grain growth, phase decomposition, or chemical inhomogeneity relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experiment requires the two sets to have identical nanoscale microstructure, but the size-based intervention would deliberately give one set smaller particles. That comparison cannot simultaneously preserve identical initial microstructure and vary particle size.
